title: Load-bearing ceramics that survive long service in air above the silica limit

concept.text: The innovation would be a ceramic or ceramic-matrix structural material that carries load for an application-relevant lifetime in flowing air at temperatures beyond the useful protective range of silica. It would retain an adherent protective surface layer while limiting loss of material and load-bearing capacity. The central achievement is the combination of oxidation protection, mechanical durability and useful lifetime under the same exposure conditions. A high melting point, a brief survival test or strength measured separately from oxidation would establish only part of that capability.

In the proposed version of this concept, oxidation produces a solid, adherent scale: a surface reaction layer that slows further attack rather than allowing the underlying structure to be consumed rapidly. Requiring the scale to remain wholly solid is an additional design constraint, not an established requirement for all successful protection. Existing approaches also use protective glass or liquid phases. Their performance is relevant progress toward durable hot structures, although it would not by itself satisfy this narrower solid-scale target.

The silica limit is a condition-dependent engineering boundary, not a universal temperature assigned to every ceramic or atmosphere. A 2021 review identifies protective oxidation above about 1700 °C as a development need beyond the barrier associated with SiC-based materials and their silica protection. That motivates the target; it does not establish a single operating cutoff or prove that the combined capability remains unavailable as of November 1, 2026.

significance.text: If demonstrated, the capability would expand the usable combination of temperature, stress and lifetime for structures exposed to oxidizing environments. Refractory diborides and carbides can retain a solid bulk material at temperatures where oxidation has already caused serious recession or damage to their protective layers. Overcoming that mismatch would make more of their high-temperature capability structurally useful. The direct benefits within the demonstrated operating range would be reduced material consumption, better shape retention and sustained load capacity; acceptably small recession would still allow some ablation.

As an application-level synthesis, potential beneficiaries include reusable leading edges, nozzles and heat-engine parts whose geometry and strength must survive repeated hot exposure. A successful loaded material section would justify component development, but would not establish a mission-ready part. Component geometry, attachments, thermal gradients and manufacturing consistency would require validation. Hypersonic vehicles and hotter turbines would also depend on aerodynamics, propulsion, cooling and system integration, so the material breakthrough alone would not establish their feasibility or performance.

The supported comparison is with the temperature constraints of silica-based protection, rather than a universal ceiling shared by nickel superalloys and SiC. Nor does this concept require operation above 3000 °C. Such operation would be a substantially harder subset of the same advance because the protective oxides themselves can melt, volatilize or lose adherence. The 2025 review gives melting points of approximately 2700 °C for ZrO2 and 2800 °C for HfO2. Those examples illustrate the difficulty of a solid scale at 3000 °C without proving that every possible oxide system must fail there.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to establish is sustained protective oxidation together with retained structural performance under simultaneous load and service-relevant exposure. The 2021 review reports inadequate oxidation resistance in the majority of the borides, carbides, MAX phases and high-entropy ceramics it surveys. The 2025 review documents substantial oxidation and ablation advances while identifying continuing challenges in long-term stability, reliability and evaluation. Together these sources establish a demanding engineering target, but not an exhaustive finding that no material has achieved it.

The protection problem concerns the products of oxidation as much as the original ceramic. The reaction layer must sufficiently limit continued attack, avoid a porous structure that leaves pathways for oxidation, and resist erosion, volatilization and loss of adherence. The 2025 review discusses porous oxide formation in carbide systems as well as glass volatilization and scale stripping. These mechanisms explain why a refractory bulk material can lose useful section thickness far below its melting point.

The mechanical and chemical requirements must also remain compatible over time. Protection that succeeds during an unstressed exposure may not establish retained strength or acceptable deformation under a sustained tensile or bending load. Conversely, good high-temperature strength measured without the relevant oxidizing exposure does not establish structural lifetime in air. The solid-scale version adds the need to demonstrate that the protective layer remains solid at operating temperature, rather than relying on a glass or liquid phase that solidifies during cooling.

A further barrier is connecting laboratory measurements to service. The 2025 review calls for improved oxidation and ablation evaluation and advanced in situ characterization to guide stable, long-life operation. Exposure duration, cycling, atmosphere and flow must be understood together with structural response. Separate records for melting point, short-term ablation resistance and mechanical properties cannot simply be combined into a demonstrated loaded-service lifetime.

current_state.text: Kane, Pint, Mitchell and Haynes’s 2021 review, “Oxidation of ultrahigh temperature ceramics: kinetics, mechanisms, and applications,” identifies the silica-related limitation of SiC-based materials and a need for protective oxidation above 1700 °C. Its abstract also describes oxidation shortcomings across the majority of the surveyed refractory ceramic families and advocates application-specific oxidation criteria. The supplied evidence for this source is the ORNL abstract record, not the full review, so it supports those broad conclusions without supplying a complete comparison of individual materials and test conditions.

“Ultra-high temperature ceramics for extreme environments,” published online on December 15, 2023 and appearing in Nature Reviews Materials 9 (2024), pages 773–789, discusses exceptional refractory properties, including melting points above 4000 °C. That figure describes material properties discussed in the abstract, not a demonstrated operating temperature in air under load. The supplied review had access to the subscription preview and abstract, while the main article body remained paywalled. General statements of promise in that preview do not establish oxidation lifetime.

The separately accessible, complete 14-page supplementary information for the Nature review provides a concrete example of scale damage. Table S3 records a ZrB2 material containing 20 vol% SiC exposed in air at 1927 °C for ten cycles of ten minutes each, with a scale described as several millimetres thick and eroded. This supports the importance of scale retention during cyclic exposure. It does not establish a general failure boundary for all UHTCs, and other temperature or pressure entries in the supplement should not be interpreted as evidence of simultaneous structural loading.

The 2025 review “Research Progress on Ultra-high Temperature Ceramic Structural Materials for Extreme Environments,” Journal of Inorganic Materials 40(10), pages 1045–1078, reports meaningful protective-scale and ablation progress. In section 3.2, it describes a modified composite with almost no damage after ten repeated ablation cycles at 2500 °C, each lasting 300 seconds. This is a reported result summarized by the review, not a demonstration newly verified here. The supplied validated review examined text spanning all 34 article pages, but did not inspect the underlying study or figure images. The inspected prose does not establish sustained applied tensile or bending stress in flowing air during those cycles.

These records show both progress and persistent durability concerns. The 2025 review separately requires high melting point and good oxidation resistance for long-duration applications, and identifies long-term stability, reliability and service-representative evaluation as continuing challenges. The supplied evidence does not establish completion of the proposed combined loaded-service demonstration. Equally, the absence of such a demonstration from this record is not proof that it does not exist. With no supplied freshness assessment, availability of the complete capability as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: test a dense ceramic or ceramic-matrix section under a stated tensile or bending stress in flowing air beyond the useful silica-protection range established for those conditions. Maintain the combined exposure for a duration justified by the intended reusable mission or maintenance interval. Require retained load capacity, acceptable deformation and recession small relative to the original load-bearing section. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not published universal standards; temperature, duration, stress and permissible damage should be chosen for the application.
completion_criteria.label: Retain load-bearing integrity for application-relevant lifetimes beyond silica protection

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol: report specimen composition, processing, density, dimensions and surface condition; actual specimen temperature; atmosphere composition and pressure; gas flow; stress history; and any heating and cooling cycles. Define the silica-protected comparison under the same relevant conditions rather than treating 1700 °C as an automatic pass–fail boundary. Measure material loss and section recession alongside deformation and residual mechanical performance. For this concept’s solid-scale constraint, establish scale composition, continuity and adherence, and use evidence capable of determining its state during hot operation rather than relying only on a cooled specimen.
completion_criteria.label: Report exposure conditions, damage, and protective scale’s hot-operation state

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope: repeat the result across specimens and manufacturing batches, with independent reproduction of the central loaded-exposure result where feasible. State the demonstrated ranges of temperature, stress, flow, duration and cycling, including observed failure boundaries. Finite tests would establish performance across that tested range, not literal universality across all air environments or service conditions. Component qualification would then require the geometry, thermal gradients and load histories relevant to a particular leading edge, nozzle or heat-engine part.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce loaded-exposure results across specimens and batches within stated limits

completion_criteria.text: A short torch test, a melting point above 3000 °C, or an unstressed coupon exposure would remain useful evidence for particular properties, but would not alone meet the proposed combined demonstration. The application-specific approach is consistent with the 2021 review’s oxidation heuristics and the 2025 review’s call for better evaluation of long-life service.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate combined performance beyond short or unstressed property tests

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CRM-01, “Room-temperature tensile ductility in bulk polycrystalline structural ceramics,” concerns deformation and damage tolerance at room temperature. CRM-02 concerns oxidation protection and structural survival during ultrahigh-temperature exposure. CRM-05, “Repeated, in-service restoration of strength after critical cracks,” could complement CRM-02 by repairing damage, but repeated strength restoration is distinct from preventing oxidative consumption and retaining a protective scale. Neither ductility nor healing alone establishes hot loaded-service lifetime.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-08, “Stoichiometric silicon-carbide fiber and composites at general industrial cost,” overlaps through ceramic-matrix structural architectures and potential manufacturing economics. Its target is affordable fiber and composite production; CRM-02 targets survival beyond the useful silica-protection range. CRM-04, “Densification of arbitrary structural ceramics without a high-temperature furnace cycle,” and CRM-11, “Net-shape additive manufacturing of fully dense technical ceramics,” address processing and geometry. They could enable production of candidate structures, but density, shape fidelity and economical fabrication do not establish protective oxidation under load.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-07, “A low-activation structural ceramic that keeps its heat transport after fusion-relevant irradiation,” shares the need to preserve useful properties in an extreme environment. Its defining constraints are irradiation, activation and heat transport, whereas CRM-02 centers on flowing-air oxidation, recession and mechanical lifetime. CRM-12, “Large transparent ceramics whose failure stress approaches theoretical strength,” shares a structural-strength concern but targets transparency, size and defect-limited strength rather than protective scale chemistry during hot service.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-03, “A ceramic electrolyte that makes lithium-metal solid-state cells ordinary technology,” CRM-06, “Ambient-pressure, room-temperature superconductivity in a useful ceramic conductor,” CRM-09, “Ceramic membranes that replace cryogenic olefin–paraffin distillation,” and CRM-10, “An earth-abundant oxide ceramic that turns sunlight and water into fuel at practical efficiency and life,” are distinct functional-material targets. They respectively concern battery operation, superconducting conduction, molecular separation and solar-fuel production. Their shared use of ceramics does not make their defining capabilities substitutes for oxidation-resistant load-bearing service.

Beyond the roster, CRM-02 overlaps with UHTC composites, protective coatings, oxidation-scale chemistry and reusable thermal protection. These approaches can contribute to the proposed capability. Their individual achievements must still be distinguished from a simultaneous demonstration of protective oxidation, retained structural performance and application-relevant lifetime, including the additional solid-scale constraint used here.

unresolved_issues: Whether any material has demonstrated the complete combination of sustained load, flowing air, operation beyond condition-specific silica protection, an adherent solid scale and application-relevant lifetime as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved.

The underlying study and figure images supporting the 2025 review’s 2500 °C repeated-ablation result were not inspected in the supplied review. Its detailed loading, flow and damage-measurement conditions remain unverified here.
The Nature review’s main body and the full 2021 oxidation review were unavailable in the supplied evidence; the accessible Nature supplement and ORNL abstract support narrower conclusions.
A particular application must still define the silica comparison, operating conditions, required lifetime, permissible recession and deformation, and reproducibility requirements.

Requiring a wholly solid scale may exclude otherwise useful glass- or liquid-assisted protection. It is retained as the proposed concept constraint, but whether it is necessary for the intended applications remains an open design question.
No supplied evidence establishes a general 3000 °C operating capability or the impossibility of achieving one with another protective chemistry.

brief.title: Ceramics that carry loads through prolonged extreme heat
possible: Reusable aircraft edges, nozzles and engine parts could keep their shape and strength through repeated exposure to hotter flowing air. Their ceramic structures would carry loads for a useful working lifetime beyond the temperatures where silica, a protective surface material, remains effective.
The ceramic would form a solid protective skin as it reacts with oxygen. That skin would stay attached and slow further attack while the structure beneath it carries weight or resists bending.
why: Some ceramics remain solid at temperatures where oxygen already eats away their surfaces. Solving that mismatch would let engineers use more of their heat resistance, with less material loss and longer retention of strength and shape.

sources.showed: Their review describes ceramics with very high melting points. Its supplement reports an eroded protective layer after repeated heating in air.
sources.cited_for: Protective surface damage can limit usefulness even when the underlying ceramic resists melting.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish a useful lifetime under sustained load in flowing air with a protective skin that stays solid.

sources.who: Kenneth A. Kane, Bruce A. Pint, David J. Mitchell and James A. Haynes
sources.showed: Their review finds inadequate resistance to oxygen attack across most ceramic families surveyed and argues that protection must be judged for each application.
sources.quote: The vast array of ultra-high and high temperature ceramic literature indicates the majority of these materials, like borides, carbides, MAX-phases, and high-entropy ceramics, fall woefully short regarding oxidation resistance.
sources.cited_for: Resistance to melting alone does not establish durable protection in hot air.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate the combined protection, sustained strength and working lifetime sought here.

sources.showed: Their review reports a modified composite, a material combining different constituents, with almost no damage after repeated tests at 2500 °C that exposed it to heat-driven material loss.
sources.cited_for: Repeated hot-exposure tests show progress in protecting ceramics against material loss.
sources.not_established: The reported result does not establish sustained pulling or bending loads in flowing air, or a protective skin that stays wholly solid.

shown: Li Xiaoxuan and colleagues report a composite with almost no damage after repeated exposure at 2500 °C. That is progress against heat-driven material loss. Sustained load capacity through the same exposure, with a protective skin that remains solid, has not been established by that result.
missing: A demonstration must combine sustained load, flowing hot air and a working lifetime beyond silica protection under the same conditions.
The protective skin must stay solid and attached during operation while limiting material loss and deformation.
The combined result must repeat across specimens and manufacturing batches, with clear limits on where it works.

milestones.label: Load capacity survives a useful working lifetime
milestones.explanation: A ceramic section would have to carry a stated load in flowing air beyond silica protection for an application-relevant lifetime. Limited thinning and deformation would establish useful structural survival.

milestones.label: Conditions, damage and the hot protective skin are established
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to document the material and exposure, compare silica protection, measure damage and strength, and establish that the skin stays solid and attached while hot. This would make the claimed protection assessable.

milestones.label: Results repeat across specimens and manufacturing batches
milestones.explanation: The loaded-exposure result would have to repeat across specimens and batches, independently where feasible, with operating and failure limits stated. This would establish reliability within a defined range.

milestones.label: Combined performance extends beyond brief or unloaded tests
milestones.explanation: Protection, load capacity and useful lifetime would have to be demonstrated together under application-relevant conditions. This would connect separate material properties to sustained structural service.

uncertain: Whether any material already achieves the complete combination remains unresolved.
Each application must define its silica comparison, required lifetime and acceptable damage.
A wholly solid protective skin may exclude useful glass or liquid protection; whether applications need that restriction remains open.

page.title: Load-bearing ultra-high-temperature ceramics in air
page.definition: Ceramic structures carry specified mechanical loads throughout a required service exposure in flowing air beyond the useful range of silica protection. Silica, silicon dioxide formed by oxidizing silicon carbide, protects within an exposure-dependent temperature range.

goal.need: An ORNL review identifies protective oxidation above 1700 °C as a need beyond silicon-carbide/silica protection. C3HARME specifies the thermal-protection conditions tabulated here for Mach 7 vehicles. Structural use requires retaining load capacity through the oxidizing exposure, rather than merely remaining below the ceramic's melting point.

figures.caption: C3HARME thermal-protection design conditions for Mach 7 vehicles
figures.note: Programme design conditions; these are not measured endurance results or universal ceramic qualification limits.

statements.quote: Materials capable of oxidizing in a protective manner at ultrahigh (>1700 °C) temperatures are needed to push beyond this barrier defined by SiC.
statements.context: The laboratory's record reproduces the review authors' statement about the temperature limitation of silicon-carbide/silica protection.

statements.quote: aiming to create a new class of Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic Matrix Composites (UHTCMCs).
statements.context: The final report describes combining fibre-reinforced ceramic matrices with ultra-high-temperature ceramics for rocket nozzles and thermal-protection tiles.

completion.title: A ceramic completes its specified loaded service life in air beyond the silica-protection range.
completion.criterion: A ceramic structural section completes an application's entire required service exposure in flowing air beyond the useful silica-protection range under the same atmosphere, pressure and flow. Applied tensile or bending load and protective oxidation act simultaneously. The section satisfies the application owner's published limits for load capacity, deformation and section recession, including required reuse cycles. The owner specifies material temperature, stress, exposure duration, gas conditions and permissible damage before testing; no universal numerical values are assigned here.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; the application owner must supply the numerical service requirements.
completion.basis: Searches of C3HARME targets and reports, DARPA MACH, ASTM C1337's public scope and ECSS readiness criteria found no common combined temperature–stress–flow–lifetime threshold. ORNL uses application-specific oxidation criteria; the 2025 review identifies stability and reliability challenges. The fallback therefore tests one complete externally specified service exposure.

milestones.title: A ceramic reaches TRL 3 by experimentally demonstrating a critical material function.
milestones.criterion: Meet ECSS technology readiness level (TRL) 3: demonstrate a critical function through analytical models supported by experiments. Related result: Chen et al. (2023) tested carbon-fibre/ZrB2–SiC with 4.9 vol% Y2O3 through ten 300 s plasma-ablation cycles at 2500 °C, separated by 120 s air cooling. They report 0.33 µm/s linear recession and 6.7% mass loss. The plasma used air plus nitrogen; the main text gives no replicate count or sustained applied mechanical load. The paper does not assign an ECSS TRL.
milestones.set_by: European Cooperation for Space Standardization, ECSS-E-HB-11A, section 5.3.3; a generic maturity criterion, not a ceramic endurance limit.
milestones.threshold_quote: Analytical and experimental critical function and/or characteristic proof-of-concept

milestones.title: An integrated ceramic laboratory model reaches TRL 4 by demonstrating its basic functions.
milestones.criterion: Meet ECSS TRL 4: an integrated laboratory model demonstrates basic functional performance with its constituent parts working together. C3HARME's final report, updated on 17 March 2021, records about 1000 specimens spanning more than 50 compositions, including discs, bars, screws and nozzle inserts, characterized at laboratory scale and explicitly labelled TRL 4. This is a programme report, not a peer-reviewed endurance result.
milestones.set_by: European Cooperation for Space Standardization, ECSS-E-HB-11A, section 5.3.4; C3HARME explicitly uses TRL 4 for its laboratory specimens.

milestones.title: A subscale ceramic component reaches TRL 5 by verifying critical functions in its relevant environment.
milestones.criterion: Meet ECSS TRL 5: verify critical functions on a subscale component in the relevant environment, with scaling effects identified. Related evidence: Sciti et al. (2025) exposed carbon-fibre/ZrB2–SiC bars to dissociated-air plasma at 2000–2200 °C before room-temperature bending. Four bars are individually tracked; two underwent two exposures. About 75–84% of initial flexural strength remained, depending on exposure and section definition. Loading occurred afterward; the paper does not assign an ECSS TRL.
milestones.set_by: European Cooperation for Space Standardization, ECSS-E-HB-11A, section 5.3.5; a generic relevant-environment gate, with application-specific performance requirements.
milestones.threshold_quote: critical function verification in a relevant environment

milestones.title: A realistically sized ceramic component reaches TRL 6 in relevant-environment system tests.
milestones.criterion: Meet C3HARME's TRL 6 target: fabricate realistically sized and shaped ceramic components, assemble them into a supporting system and validate them in the relevant environment. The final report records TRL 5/6 for thermal-protection tiles and TRL 6/7 for rocket nozzles following arc-jet and motor ground tests. Prototype counts and combined loaded lifetimes are unstated. These programme-reported results are not peer reviewed and do not establish the full flowing-air service-life test.
milestones.set_by: European Commission Horizon 2020 C3HARME, published project objective; the target was written for rocket nozzles and thermal-protection tiles.
milestones.threshold_quote: rocket nozzles and TPS tiles with realistic dimensions and shape will be fabricated, assembled into a suitable system, and validated in a relevant ambient

not_found: No published demonstration establishing simultaneous sustained load, protective oxidation and the specified service lifetime beyond the condition-specific silica range was located.
No programme or standard located requires the protective oxidation layer to remain wholly solid.
The full Nature review and the full 2021 oxidation review could not be opened.
The 2025 review's PDF could not be retrieved; its abstract and figure captions were accessible.
Sciti et al. describe four individually tracked arc-jet bars but elsewhere mention six exposed bars; the total exposed specimen count remains unresolved.

results.finding: One assembled UHTCMC thermal protection tile, 194 mm × 240 mm × 4 mm, was tested in a plasma wind tunnel.
results.detail: The tile included ceramic standoffs, screws and nuts. The paper reports that the assembly was tested but does not state its functional performance or establish TRL 4.
results.quote:
A TPS tile 
entirely made in sintered UHTCMC with dimensions 194 mm × 240 mm × 4 mm is shown equipped with 
UHTCMC standoffs assembled through UHTCMC screws and nuts, according to design presented in Fig. 1. 
The assembled model was tested in the hypersonic L3K plasma wind tunnel facility of DLR in Cologne [46].

results.finding: UHTCMC thermal protection assemblies from 8 material formulations survived repeated arc-jet tests; assembly sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The authors report achieving TRL 5 after upscaling to a tile assembly. The text does not establish ECSS TRL 5, identify scaling effects, or specify mechanical loads carried during exposure.
results.quote: The assemblies survived repeated tests without damage nor relevant erosion, thus achieving the objective Technology Readiness Level of 5.

results.finding: C3HARME rocket-nozzle prototypes, number unstated, reached a reported TRL of 6/7.
results.detail: The programme reports solid-rocket-motor ground tests and relevant pressure and temperature resistance. Prototype counts and combined loaded lifetimes are unstated; the report does not establish the full flowing-air service-life test.
results.quote: Overall C3HARME started with a Technological Readiness Level of 3 and reached TRL 5/6 for TPS tiles and 6/7 for rocket nozzles in propulsion.
